Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 11–12:

﴿Why do you not trust us with Joseph?﴾ That is: you do not fear for him from us. The Seven Readers recited "تأمنا" (ta'manna) with idgham (assimilation) and ishmam (partial vowel-suggestion), because its original form is with a dammah on the first nun.

﴿Let him go out tomorrow and play and enjoy himself (yarta')﴾ Whoever recites it with a kasrah on the ʿayn (yarta'i) takes it from ar-ri'y (ar-ri'y, pasturing), i.e., from the pasturing of camels, or from one of them pasturing for another and guarding him. Whoever recites it with sukun (yarta') takes it from ar-rat' (ar-rat', dwelling in abundance and luxury), and the tā' in this case is original, and the form of the verb is yaf'al; its form according to the first reading is yaf'il (or nafta'il in the sense given).

Whoever recites "yarta'u wa yal'ab" with the yā' (yā'), the pronoun refers to Joseph. Whoever recites with the nūn (narta'u wa nal'ab), the pronoun refers to the speakers, who are his brothers. They said "nal'ab" (we play) only because at that time they were not prophets, and play was permissible for training, like racing horses.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 15:

﴿وَأَجْمَعُوۤاْ﴾ means: they resolved (ʿazamū). The answer to "lammā" (when) is omitted. It is also said that the answer is "wa-ajmaʿū" itself, or that the "wa" is extra, so that the sense is "and We revealed" (wa-awḥaynā). ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَآ﴾: this revelation may be through an angel, or by inspiration (ilhām). The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to Yusuf, though it is also said to refer to Yaʿqub; the first view is the correct one. ﴿وَهُمْ لاَ يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "latunabbi'annahum", meaning: they will not perceive at the time you inform them, in which case the address is to Yusuf (peace be upon him). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verses 17–18:

﴿We go racing﴾, meaning: we run on our feet to see which of us outruns the other. ﴿And you will not believe us﴾, meaning: you will not accept what we say as true. ﴿Even if we were truthful﴾, meaning: you would not believe us even if we were among those who speak the truth to you, so how much less when you accuse us. It was also said that the meaning is: do not believe us even if we are truthful in this statement, and that this is said by them as a form of deception (mughalata). The first interpretation is more evident. ﴿They came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, meaning: blood that is a lie (dhu kadhib), or the noun kadhib is used as an adjective for emphasis. It is narrated that they smeared his shirt with the blood of a young goat (jady) and said to Ya'qub (Jacob): "This is his blood on his shirt." He said to them: "How is it that the wolf ate him yet did not tear his shirt?" By this he inferred that they were lying. ﴿Made seem fair﴾, meaning: adorned. ﴿So patience is fitting (sabrun jamil)﴾ is a resolve he made within himself to be patient. Its nominative case (irfa') is because it is a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), with the implied meaning: "fitting patience is best," or it is a predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate) of an implied subject, with the meaning: "my matter is fitting patience."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verses 19–20:

﴿And a caravan came⦆ It is narrated that this caravan was from Madyan, and it was said: they were Bedouin Arabs. ﴿Their water-drawer (wārid)﴾ The wārid is the one who draws water for a group. Al-Suhayli reported that the name of this wārid was Malik ibn Du'ar, from the ancient Arabs (al-'Arab al-'Ariba), and that he had no children, so he asked Yusuf to pray for him to have offspring, and he prayed for him, and God granted him twelve sons, each of whom became the ancestor of a tribe. ﴿He said: "O good news!"﴾ That is, he called out "good news," as you would say "O regret!" and he attributed it to himself. It is also read "yā bushrā" with the first-person pronoun elided, and the meaning is the same. It was said that according to this reading he called out to a man among them named Bushra, but this is far-fetched. When the wārid lowered his bucket into the well, Yusuf caught hold of it, and then he said: "O my good news! This is a boy." ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise⦆ The subject pronoun refers to the caravan and the object pronoun refers to Yusuf; that is, they hid him from the company, or they said to them: "A people entrusted him to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." ﴿And they sold him﴾ That is, they sold him. The pronoun likewise refers to those who took him. It was said that the pronoun refers to Yusuf's brothers, and that they came back to him and said to the caravan: "This is our slave." ﴿For a paltry price﴾ That is, less than its true value. It was also said that bakhs here means injustice. ﴿A few dirhams counted﴾ This is an expression for their small number. ﴿And they were﴾ The pronoun refers to those who took him, or to his brothers.

﴿And the one who bought him said﴾ meaning the ʿAzīz, who was the chamberlain and treasurer of the king. Al-Suhaylī said: his name was Qiṭfīr. ﴿from Egypt﴾ is the well-known land, and that is why it is not declined (lam yanṣarif, i.e. it is treated as a diptote, not taking nunation). **Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 23:**

﴿He reached his full strength (bulugh ashuddahu)﴾. It was said: al-ashudd (the full strength, *ashudd*) is puberty (*bulugh*). It was said: it is eighteen years. It was said: thirty-three. It was said: forty. ﴿Judgment (hukman)﴾: it is wisdom (*hikmah*) and prophethood. ﴿She, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself (wa-raawadathu allati huwa fi baytiha 'an nafsihi)﴾, meaning: she asked from him what a man would ask from a woman. She was Zulaykha, the wife of al-'Aziz. ﴿And she locked the doors (wa-ghallaqati al-abwab)﴾: it is reported that there were seven doors. ﴿Hayta laka (Come hither)﴾ is an *ism fi'l* (a noun functioning as a verb, meaning "come" or "approach"). It is read with the *ha'* vowelled with a fatha or a kasra, and the *ta'* with a fatha or a damma. The meaning of all of these is one. The vowel on the *ta'* is for *bina'* (indeclinability). As for the one who reads it with a hamza, it is a verb from *tahayya'tu* (I prepared myself), like your saying *ji'tu* (I came). ﴿Ma'adha Allah (God forbid!)﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the meaning is: I seek refuge in God. ﴿Innahu rabbi (Indeed, he is my lord)﴾: the pronoun may refer to God, the Exalted, or to the one who bought him, because a master is called *rabb*. So the meaning is: it is not fitting for me to betray him. ﴿Innahu la yuflihu al-zalimun (Indeed, the wrongdoers do not prosper)﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter and the situation (*al-amr wa-l-sha'n*). It is also possible that the pronoun in the first case is of this type.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 24:

﴿And indeed she desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord.﴾ People have spoken at great length about this verse, to the point that they have composed whole books on it. Among them are those who go to excess and those who fall short. Some made the desire of the woman and the desire of Yusuf refer to the act she sought, and they related reports about his sitting between her thighs, the untying of the drawstring, and other such things, which should not be affirmed because their transmission is weak and because the prophets are free of such things. Others said that she desired him so that she might strike him for refusing her, and that he desired her so that he might kill her or strike her to repel her; this is far-fetched, since his words "had he not seen the proof of his Lord" refute it. Others made her desire for him refer to her intention, and his desire for her to be his repelling her; this too is far-fetched, because it contradicts the flow of the discourse. The correct view, God willing, is that she desired him in the sense of her intention, and he likewise desired her, but he did not resolve upon it and did not reach what was mentioned about untying the drawstring and other things. Rather, his desire was a passing thought that crossed his heart, which he did not obey or follow, but he hastened to repentance and to abandoning that passing thought until he erased it from his heart when he saw the proof of his Lord. This does not detract from the infallibility of the prophets, because the intention to commit a sin is not itself a sin and is no defect in him in that respect, for whoever intends a sin and then leaves it, a good deed is recorded for him. ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord.﴾ Its answer is omitted, its implied sense being: had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have mingled with her. It was omitted because his words "he desired her" indicate it. It has been said that "he desired her" is the answer, but this is weak, because the answer of "lawla" does not precede it. Scholars differed about the proof he saw. It was said: Jibril called to him, "O Yusuf, will you be recorded among the prophets and act like the foolish?" It was said: he saw Ya'qub warning him. It was said: he reflected and gained insight. It was said: he saw that Zulaykha had covered the face of an idol of hers out of shame, so he said, "I have more right to be ashamed before God." ﴿Thus, that We might turn away﴾: the kaf is in a place of accusative, governed by a hidden verb; the meaning is: We made him firm with such firmness, or in a place of nominative, meaning: the matter is like that. ﴿Evil and immorality﴾: the betrayal of his master and falling into adultery. ﴿The sincere servants﴾: it was read with a fatha on the lam wherever it occurs, meaning those whom God purified for His obedience, and with a kasra, meaning those who made their religion sincerely for God.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 12, verses 25–29:**

﴿And they both raced to the door﴾. Its meaning: each of them outran the other to the door. He intended to go out and flee from her, and she intended to hold him back. If it is asked, "How does he say here *al-bab* (the door) in the singular, when he has said in the plural, *wa-ghullqat al-abwab* (and the doors were locked)?" the answer is that what is meant here is the *barrani* door (the outer door), which is the exit from the house. ﴿And she tore his shirt from behind﴾, that is, she cut it from behind, because she grabbed his shirt from his back to hold him back, so the shirt was torn. *Al-qadd* is cutting lengthwise, and *al-qatt* is cutting crosswise. ﴿And they found her husband at the door﴾, that is, they found her husband at the door. ﴿She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾ When she saw the disgrace, she reversed the matter and claimed that Yusuf had sought to seduce her. She mentioned the penalty for anyone who does such a thing in general terms, and did not explicitly name Yusuf, since he was included in the generality, and on the basis that the sin was established against him by her claim. *Ma* in *ma jaza'u* may be either a negative particle or an interrogative.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah Yusuf (12), verses 36–37, from al-Tashil:

﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ That is, two youths. It was said: here there is an necessary omission, namely "so they imprisoned him." It was also said: they saw these dreams as true. ﴿"Indeed, I see myself pressing wine."﴾ It was said concerning this: he called grapes "wine" because of what they would become. It was also said: this is the dialect (lughah) of a people. ﴿"Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers."﴾ It was said: its meaning is in the interpretation of dreams. It was also said: it refers to his kindness toward the people of the prison. ﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision that you are given except that I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you."﴾ The verse implies that he described himself to them as possessing abundant knowledge, so as to make that a means of calling them to the Oneness of God. There are two views on it. The first is that he said he would inform them of every food that would come to them in the world before it came, and this is of the reports of the unseen, which is the miracle of the prophets. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 40–42:

﴿O my two companions of the prison﴾ He attributed them to the prison either because they dwelt in it or because they were his companions in it, as if he had said: "O my two companions in the prison." ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?﴾ (verse) He called them to the Oneness of Allah and established the proof against them, out of desire for their faith. ﴿You worship besides Him only names﴾ He placed the names here in the position of the named things, and the meaning is: you named what does not deserve divinity "gods," and then you worshipped them. ﴿of no authority﴾ That is, no proof or evidence. ﴿One of you will give his lord wine to drink﴾ meaning the king. ﴿And he said to the one he thought would be saved of the two: "Mention me to your lord."﴾ The word "thought" (ẓanna) here may carry the sense of certainty, because His saying "the matter has been decided" requires that, or it may retain its own meaning, since it concerns the interpretation of a dream, which is a matter of conjecture. ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾ meaning the king. ﴿But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾ It was said: the pronoun refers to Joseph, meaning that he forgot at that time to mention Allah, and hoped for someone other than Allah, so Allah punished him for that by remaining in the prison. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the one of the two who was saved, namely the cupbearer, meaning that he forgot the mention of Joseph before his lord, and he attributed the mention to "his lord" since Joseph was with him; and "lord" on this interpretation means the king. ﴿For several years﴾ Bidʿ (a few, a small number) ranges from three to ten, and it was said: up to nine. It is related that Joseph, peace be upon him, was imprisoned for five years at first, then after his saying that, he was imprisoned for seven years.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 43:

﴿And the king said﴾ He was the king of Egypt, whom the Aziz (the minister) had served as an attendant. His name was Rayyan ibn al-Walid. It is also said: Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan. He was one of the Pharaohs. It is also said that he was the Pharaoh of Moses, who lived four hundred years until Moses reached him, but this is far-fetched. ﴿Indeed, I see﴾ in a dream ﴿seven fat cows, devoured by seven lean ones﴾ i.e., weak, in extreme emaciation. ﴿O chiefs﴾ an address to his companions and the people of his realm. ﴿Explain to me my dream, if you are able to interpret dreams.﴾ i.e., you know its interpretation. It is said: "'abarta al-ru'ya" (with the ba' lightened), and some have denied the doubled form (ʿabbara), though it is attested among the Arabs. The lam has been placed before the object because of what precedes the verb. ﴿They said: "Confused dreams"﴾ i.e., their jumbled and false elements, and whatever in them arises from the soul's talk or the whisperings of Satan, such that it cannot be interpreted. The root meaning of adghath is what is gathered from mixed herbs; its singular is dhigh\u1e6d. If it is asked: why did he say adghath ahlam (in the plural) when the dream was single? The answer is that this is like your saying "So-and-so rides horses," even if he rides only one mare. ﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams.﴾ They may mean either the interpretation of false dreams, or the interpretation of dreams in general, and the latter is more apparent.

﴿And the one of the two who was saved said﴾: he was the king's cupbearer. ﴿and remembered after a period﴾, meaning after some time, ﴿Joseph: O truthful one (al-Siddiq)﴾. There is a necessary omitted element to be supplied before it, which is: "So they sent him, and he said: O Joseph." He was called al-Siddiq because his truthfulness had been tested in interpreting dreams and other matters. Al-siddiq is an intensive form (mubalagha) derived from al-sidq (truthfulness). ﴿Give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows﴾, meaning concerning one who saw seven fat cows. The king had seen seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and he was amazed at how the lean ones overcame them and how they went into their bellies. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verses 52–55:

﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret.﴾ It has been said that this is part of the speech of the wife of the chief minister (al-Aziz), connected to what precedes it. On this view, the pronouns in "yaʿlam" (he may know) and "akhnhu" (I betrayed him) refer to Joseph, peace be upon him. That is: so that Joseph may know that I did not lie about him in his absence. The reference of "dhalika" (that) is to his refraining from leaving the prison until his innocence becomes clear.

﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾. It is also disputed whether this is the speech of the wife of the chief minister or the speech of Joseph. If it is her speech, then it is a confession upon a confession. If it is his speech, then it is an acknowledgment of what he had been struck by in his heart as a passing thought, not as a resolve or intention. He said this in all circumstances, out of humility.

﴿Indeed, the soul is certainly inclined to evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy.﴾ "Al-nafs" (the soul) here is generic, and souls are of three kinds: the commanding soul inclined to evil (al-ammarah bi-l-su'), the self-reproaching soul (al-lawwamah), which blames its owner, and the tranquil soul (al-mutma'innah). "Illa" (except) is an exception from "al-nafs," since it carries the sense of "souls." That is: the souls upon which mercy has been shown, namely the tranquil soul. On this reading, "ma" (what) in "ma rahima" means "alladhi" (those who). It is also possible that it is temporal, meaning: except at the time of God's mercy.

﴿Bring him to me, I will take him for myself exclusively.﴾ That is: I will make him my special companion and my chosen one. He first said, "Bring him to me," but when his condition became clear to him, he said, "I will take him for myself exclusively."

﴿So when he spoke to him, he said: Indeed, today you are with us established and trustworthy.﴾ That is: when he saw the excellence of his speech and recognized the abundance of his intellect and knowledge, he said: "Indeed, today you are with us established and trustworthy." "Makin" (established, firmly placed) derives from "tamkin" (empowerment), and "amin" (trustworthy) derives from "amanah" (trust).

﴿[Joseph] said: Appoint me over the treasuries of the land﴾. When Joseph understood from the king that he wanted him to manage affairs and to rely on him, he said this. He sought the office only out of desire for justice, the upholding of truth, and kindness. This king was an unbeliever, and from this it is inferred that it is permissible for a virtuous man to work for a wicked man if he knows that he can set right some matters. It has also been said that the king became a Muslim, and by his words "the treasuries of the land" he meant the land of Egypt, since the king had no other domain. "Khaza'in" (treasuries) refers to everything stored, whether food, wealth, or other things.

﴿Indeed I am a knowing guardian.﴾ These are two attributes that cover all aspects of knowledge of and proper management of the treasuries. It has also been said: "guardian" in the sense of keeping accounts, "knowing" of languages. The wording is more general than that. From this it is inferred that it is permissible for a man to make himself known and to praise himself with the truth when he seeks office and when there is benefit in doing so.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 58–61:

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verses 62–66:

﴿And he said to his servants (fityan)﴾ The plural of fata, which means a servant, whether free or slave. ﴿Put their merchandise (bidā'atahum) into their saddlebags (rihalihim)﴾ He commanded that they put the merchandise with which they had bought food from him into their sacks. ﴿So that they may recognize it (la'allahum ya'rifunaha)﴾ That is, so that they may recognize the kindness and the generosity in returning the merchandise to them, and the pronoun does not refer to the merchandise. ﴿So that they may return (la'allahum yarji'un)﴾ That is, so that their recognition of it may move them to return, and the purpose of returning the merchandise to them along with the food was to win them over through kindness to them. ﴿The measure is denied us (muni'a minna al-kayl)﴾ This is a reference to his saying: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (kayl) for you with me﴾ [Yusuf: 60], so it is a fear of being denied in the future. ﴿We will be given measure (naktal)﴾ its form is naftaʻil from al-kayl (measuring). ﴿What do we desire (ma nabghi)﴾ "Ma" is interrogative, and nabghi means we seek. The meaning is: what thing do we seek after this generosity, namely the return of the merchandise along with the food? It may also be that "ma" is negative, and nabghi is from al-baghy: that is, we do not transgress against our brother and we do not lie to the king. ﴿And we will provide for our family (wa namir ahlana)﴾ That is, we will bring them food. ﴿And we will gain an extra camel-load (wa nazdad kayla ba'ir)﴾ They mean the camel-load of their brother, since Yusuf would not give anyone more than one camel-load of food per person; so he gave them ten camel-loads and withheld the eleventh because its owner was absent, until he should come. The ba'ir is the camel (jamal). ﴿That is a small measure (dhalika kayl yasir)﴾ If the reference is to the loads, then the meaning is that they are few and will not suffice them unless a camel-load is added to them; and if the reference is to the camel-load, then the meaning is that it is easy for Yusuf, that is, small in his possession or easy for him, so he does not withhold it from them. ﴿Until you give me a solemn covenant from God (hatta tu'tunni mawthiqan min Allah)﴾ He wanted them to swear an oath to him, and "wa latatunnahu bihi" is the answer to the oath. ﴿Unless you are overpowered (illa an yuhata bikum)﴾ That is, unless you are overcome so that you are unable to bring him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 73–76:

﴿They said: "By Allah, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ That is, they called upon their knowledge of what had become apparent to them of their (the brothers') integrity in entering their land, to the point that they would place stones (al-akimma) in the mouths of their camels so that they would not reach the crops of the people. ﴿They said: "What is its requital if you are liars?"﴾ That is, the young men of Yusuf said: "What is the requital of the one who takes the drinking-cup, if you are lying in your statement: 'We were not thieves'?" The pronoun in His saying "its requital" refers to the act of taking (al-akhdh) that is understood from the speech. ﴿They said: "Its requital is that one in whose saddlebag it is found—he is its requital."﴾ The meaning is that the brothers of Yusuf gave a ruling on what they were asked about, and they said: the requital of a thief is that he be enslaved and seized for the theft. As for the i'rab (grammatical analysis), it allows two possibilities. The first: that the first "jaza'uhu" is a subject (mubtada'), "man" is a second subject, and it is either conditional or relative, and its predicate is "fahuwa jaza'uhu," and the clause is the predicate of the first "jaza'uhu." The second possibility: that "man" is the predicate of the first subject, with an elided modifier (mudaf), its estimate being: "its requital is the seizure of the one found in his saddlebag," and the speech is complete. Then He said "fahuwa jaza'uhu," meaning: this ruling is its requital. ﴿And thus We requite the wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf: 41] is from the speech of the brothers of Yusuf, meaning: this is our ruling concerning the thief. This ruling was in place at the beginning of Islam, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the cutting off of hands. ﴿So he began with their bags﴾ This is a means of carrying out the scheme and removing suspicion. ﴿Then he extracted it from his brother's bag﴾ so that by this it would be valid for him to keep his brother with him. The word "al-sa', the drinking-cup" was made feminine in this place because it is a watering-vessel (siqaya), or because al-sa' is both masculine and feminine.

﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾ That is, We arranged for him this arrangement. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ That is, under his legal system or custom, because the requital for a thief in his [the king's] judgment was only that he be beaten and that the fine be doubled upon him. But he ruled in this matter according to the family of Ya'qub. ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ That is, the elevation is by knowledge, as evidenced by what follows. ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is One All-Knowing﴾ That is, above every scholar is one who is more knowledgeable than him among mankind, or Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verse 77:

﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before."﴾ The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the brothers of Yusuf, and they gestured toward Yusuf. The meaning of their words is: if Binyamin steals, then his brother Yusuf had stolen before him. This matter, they meant, came only from the two sons of Rahil, our mother, and by this they intended to remove the blame from themselves and to cast it upon Yusuf and his full brother. Scholars differed about the theft with which they charged Yusuf, in three opinions. The first: his paternal aunt had raised him, and his father wished to take him from her, but she loved him and could not bear to be parted from him, so she put on him a belt of hers, then claimed that he had taken it, and by this she enslaved him, and he remained with her until she died. The second: that he took an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather and broke it. The third: that he used to take food from his father's house and give it to the needy.

﴿So Yusuf kept it hidden within himself﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun refers to the statement that follows, which is his saying: "You are worse in position," meaning he said it in response to their saying: "You are worse in position." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun refers to the resentment he felt within himself at their saying: "a brother of his had stolen before," and he concealed his dislike of their statement, then confronted them openly with his saying: "You are worse in position," meaning because of the evil of your deeds.

﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you describe﴾, an indication of their lying in what they attributed to him of theft.

Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil*, on Surah 12, verses 78–83:

﴿Indeed, he has a father, an elderly old man.﴾ (This is) an appeal for pity. They had informed him of his father's intense love for him. ﴿So take one of us in his place.﴾ (This is) by way of surety, as a pledge and in submission. This is the more apparent reading, because of his saying: ﴿God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers.﴾ That is, you have done good to us in what you did with us before, or (it is) in general. ﴿They despaired of him﴾, that is, they gave up hope. ﴿They withdrew to confer privately﴾, that is, they withdrew from others and conferred with one another in secret. The word najiyy may be used in the sense of munājī (one who confides), or as a verbal noun. ﴿The eldest of them said﴾: it was said that the eldest of them in age was Rubil, and it was said that the eldest of them in judgment was Shim'un, and it was said (he was) Yahuda. ﴿And before this, you neglected Joseph.﴾ The particle "mā" may carry several possibilities. First: that it is redundant (zā'ida). Second: that it is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, its place being nominative as the subject, the sense being: "Your neglect of Joseph occurred before." Third: that it is a relative (mawṣūla) particle, its place likewise nominative in this way. **"O my sons, go"** (Yā banīya idhhabū): meaning, go to the land in which you left your two brothers. **"And search out information about Yusuf and his brother"** (fa-tahassasū min Yūsuf wa-akhīh): meaning, seek to learn news of the two of them. Al-tahassus (searching out, sensing) is seeking a thing through the senses: hearing and sight. He did not mention the third son because he remained there by his own choice, and because Yusuf and his brother were dearer to him.

**"And do not despair of the mercy of Allah"** (wa-lā tay'asū min rawh Allāh): meaning, of the mercy of Allah. **"Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people"** (innahu lā yay'asu min rawh Allāh illā al-qawm al-kāfirūn): despair was attributed to the attribute of the disbeliever only because its cause is denying Lordship, or ignorance of Allah's attributes, such as His power, grace and mercy.

**"When they entered upon him"** (falammā dakhalū 'alayh): meaning, upon Yusuf. It is also said that this is elided, its implied sense being: so they returned to Egypt. **"Adversity"** (al-durr): they meant by it famine, or grief over their brothers. **"With goods of little value"** (bi-biḍā'a muzjāh): they meant the dirhams with which they had come to buy food. Al-muzjāh means few or little; it is also said: poor quality; and it is said: deficient. It is also said that their merchandise had been goods (ʿurūḍ), and therefore they said this.

**"And give us charity"** (wa-taṣaddaq 'alaynā): it is said they meant, by what lies between good dirhams and their own dirhams [from above]. It is also said: fill up the measure for us, which is our due, and add to our due; they called the addition charity. This implies that charity was lawful for the prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: give us charity by returning our brother to us.

**"Indeed, Allah rewards those who give charity"** (inna Allāh yajzī al-mutaṣaddiqīn): al-Naqqāsh said: this is of the ambiguous expressions (al-maʿārīḍ), for they believed he was a disbeliever, since they did not recognise him, so they thought he was upon the religion of the people of Egypt. Had they said, "Indeed Allah will reward you for your charity," they would have lied; so they said a phrase that suggests they meant him, while they did not mean him.

Al-tahassus (searching out, sensing) is seeking a thing through the senses: hearing and sight. He did not mention the third son because he remained there by his own choice, and because Yusuf and his brother were dearer to him.

**"And do not despair of the mercy of Allah"** (wa-lā tay'asū min rawh Allāh): meaning, of the mercy of Allah. **"Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people"** (innahu lā yay'asu min rawh Allāh illā al-qawm al-kāfirūn): despair was attributed to the attribute of the disbeliever only because its cause is denying Lordship, or ignorance of Allah's attributes, such as His power, grace and mercy.

**"When they entered upon him"** (falammā dakhalū 'alayh): meaning, upon Yusuf. It is also said that this is elided, its implied sense being: so they returned to Egypt. **"Adversity"** (al-durr): they meant by it famine, or grief over their brothers. **"With goods of little value"** (bi-biḍā'a muzjāh): they meant the dirhams with which they had come to buy food. Al-muzjāh means few or little; it is also said: poor quality; and it is said: deficient. It is also said that their merchandise had been goods (ʿurūḍ), and therefore they said this.

**"And give us charity"** (wa-taṣaddaq 'alaynā): it is said they meant, by what lies between good dirhams and their own dirhams [from above]. It is also said: fill up the measure for us, which is our due, and add to our due; they called the addition charity. This implies that charity was lawful for the prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: give us charity by returning our brother to us.

**"Indeed, Allah rewards those who give charity"** (inna Allāh yajzī al-mutaṣaddiqīn): al-Naqqāsh said: this is of the ambiguous expressions (al-maʿārīḍ), for they believed he was a disbeliever, since they did not recognise him, so they thought he was upon the religion of the people of Egypt. Had they said, "Indeed Allah will reward you for your charity," they would have lied; so they said a phrase that suggests they meant him, while they did not mean him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verses 89–92:

﴿He said, "Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?"﴾ When they complained to him, he felt pity for them and made himself known to them. It is reported that he was speaking to them while his face was veiled with a face-cloth (lithām). Then he removed the veil so that they would recognize him. By his words "what you did to Joseph and his brother," he meant the separation between them in childhood, the harm they caused Joseph, and their mistreatment of his brother after him, for they used to humiliate him and revile him. ﴿When you were ignorant﴾ is an excuse on their behalf. It may mean that he intends their ignorance of the ugliness of what they did, or the ignorance of youth (jahl al-shabāb). ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ It is recited with the interrogative and the declarative forms. The declarative form is on the basis that they recognized him. The interrogative form is on the basis that they recognized him; the interrogative form is on the basis that they suspected he was him but did not verify it. ﴿Whoever is mindful of God and patient﴾. It was said that he meant whoever is mindful of God by abandoning sin and is patient in prison, though the wording is more general than that. ﴿God has preferred you over us﴾, that is, He has favored you. ﴿Indeed we were sinners﴾, that is, disobedient. In their words there is both an appeal for pity and an acknowledgment of guilt. ﴿No reproach will be upon you today﴾ is a gracious pardon. Tathrīb means rebuke and punishment. His saying "today" refers back to what precedes it, so one stops at "you" (ʿalaykum), and it is connected to tathrīb, or to what is implied in ʿalaykum of the sense of settledness (al-istiqrār). It was also said that it is connected to yaghfiru (may He forgive), but this is far-fetched, because it would be a judgment imposed upon God. Rather, yaghfiru is a supplication. It is as if he had waived his own right by saying "no reproach will be upon you today," and then he called upon God to forgive them his right.

﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. It is related that this shirt belonged to Ibrahim, which Allah clothed him with when he was brought out of the Fire. It was one of the garments of Paradise. It then passed to Ishaq, then to Ya'qub, and then Ya'qub gave it to Yusuf. This requires a chain of transmission (isnad) that can be relied upon. The apparent meaning is that it was Yusuf's own shirt, like anyone's shirt. ﴿It will return him to sight﴾. The apparent meaning is that he knew this through a revelation from Allah. ﴿When the caravan set out﴾, meaning it left Egypt heading toward Ya'qub. ﴿Their father said: Indeed I smell the scent of Yusuf﴾. Ya'qub was in Bayt al-Maqdis, and he smelled the shirt's scent though there was a great distance between them. ﴿Unless you think me senile﴾, meaning you blame me or dismiss what I say. It was also said that the meaning is: you say, "Your mind has gone," because al-fannad is senility (al-kharaf). ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾, meaning your departure from what is right, due to your excessive love for Yusuf in the past. ﴿When the bearer of good news arrived﴾. It is related that the bearer of good news was Yahudha, because he had brought the bloodied shirt. So he said to his brothers: "I went to him with the shirt of sorrow (al-qarha), so let me go to him with the shirt of joy (al-farha)." ﴿He said: I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾. He promised them that he would seek forgiveness for them. It was said that he postponed it until the pre-dawn (al-sahar), because supplication is answered at that time. It was also said that he postponed it until Friday night. ﴿When they entered upon Yusuf﴾. Here there are omitted elements that the context indicates, namely: Ya'qub set out with his family until they reached Yusuf. ﴿He took his two parents to himself﴾, meaning he embraced them. By "the two parents" he meant his father and his mother. It was also said he meant his father and his maternal aunt, because his mother had died, and on this view he called the aunt "mother." ﴿If Allah wills﴾ refers to the security mentioned in His words, ﴿secure﴾.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 12, verses 99–101:

﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾, i.e., upon the couch of kingship. ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾. Prostration among them was a greeting and an honour, not worship. ﴿And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before."﴾ That is, when he saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon prostrating to him. The time between his vision and the appearance of its interpretation was eighty years, and it is said forty. ﴿"He was kind to me."﴾ It is said: one says "ahsana ilayhi" and "ahsana bihi" (he was good to him). ﴿"He brought me out of the prison."﴾ He did not say "brought me out of the well," for two reasons. The first: mentioning the well would bring shame upon his brothers and remind them of what they had done, so he left it out out of respect for them. The second: he came out of the well into slavery, and out of the prison into kingship, so the blessing through him was greater. ﴿"And brought you from the desert."﴾ i.e., from the badw (the desert), and they were owners of camels and sheep, so he counted their coming to the settled region among the blessings. ﴿"After Satan had incited discord."﴾ i.e., corrupted and led astray. ﴿"Truly He is Gracious to whom He wills."﴾ i.e., subtle in the management of what He wills among affairs. ﴿"of the kingdom"﴾: the min here is partitive, since he was given only part of the kingdom of this world, indeed only part of the kingdom of Egypt. ﴿"Let me die in submission"﴾: when he enumerated the blessings that God had bestowed upon him, he longed to meet his Lord and the righteous among his predecessors and others, so he asked for death. It is also said that this is not a supplication for death; rather, he asked that God complete His blessings upon him by causing him to die in Islam when his appointed time comes.

The second: he came out of the well into slavery, and out of the prison into kingship, so the blessing through him was greater. ﴿"And brought you from the desert."﴾ i.e., from the badw (the desert), and they were owners of camels and sheep, so he counted their coming to the settled region among the blessings. ﴿"After Satan had incited discord."﴾ i.e., corrupted and led astray. ﴿"Truly He is Gracious to whom He wills."﴾ i.e., subtle in the management of what He wills among affairs. ﴿"of the kingdom"﴾: the min here is partitive, since he was given only part of the kingdom of this world, indeed only part of the kingdom of Egypt. ﴿"Let me die in submission"﴾: when he enumerated the blessings that God had bestowed upon him, he longed to meet his Lord and the righteous among his predecessors and others, so he asked for death. It is also said that this is not a supplication for death; rather, he asked that God complete His blessings upon him by causing him to die in Islam when his appointed time comes.

It was also said that it refers to the people of Makkah. ﴿Even if you were eager, they would not be believers﴾: a parenthetical clause, meaning they will not believe, even if you were eager for their faith. ﴿And you do not ask them for any wage for it﴾, i.e., you do not ask them for a wage for faith, so that it would burden them because of that, and its meaning is the same wherever it occurs. ﴿And how many a sign﴾, meaning the creatures and events that point to Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him﴾: it was revealed concerning the pagan Arabs who acknowledge Allah yet worship others alongside Him. Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 12, verses 108–109:

﴿Say, "This is my way: I invite to Allah with insight (ʿalā baṣīrah), I and whoever follows me."﴾ — an indication of the Sharia of Islam. ﴿I invite to Allah with insight﴾, i.e., I invite people to the worship of Allah, and I am upon insight into my affair and a clear proof. ﴿I and whoever follows me﴾: "I" is an emphasis for the pronoun in "I invite"; "whoever follows me" is conjoined to it, and "upon insight" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It has also been said: "I" is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and "upon insight" is its predicate (khabar). On this view one stops at His saying "I invite to Allah," but this is weak. ﴿And glory be to Allah﴾: its implied sense is "and I say, 'Glory be to Allah.'" ﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾: a refutation of those who denied that the Prophet could be a human being. It has been said that it also contains an indication that He did not send a messenger from among women. ﴿From the people of the towns﴾: i.e., from the people of cities, not from the people of the desert (bawādī), for Allah did not send a messenger from the desert dwellers because of their harshness (jafāʾ).

Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil*, on Surah 12, verses 110–111:

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾ is connected in meaning to His words "We did not send before you except men" up to His words "the outcome of those before them." Their despair may refer to the faith of their people or to victory. The first is better.

﴿And they thought that they had been denied﴾ is read with the letter dhal (ذ) both doubled and single. With the doubled reading, the pronouns in "thought" and "denied" refer to the messengers. The word *zann* (thought) may keep its ordinary meaning, or it may mean *yaqin* (certainty): that is, the messengers knew that their people had denied them, so they despaired of their faith. With the single reading, the two pronouns refer to the people to whom they were sent. That is, they thought that the messengers had lied about what they claimed, namely the message, or about being given victory over them.

﴿In their stories﴾: the pronoun refers to the messengers in general, or to Yusuf and his brothers.

﴿It was not a narration that could be invented﴾: this means the Qur'an.

﴿But it is a confirmation of what was before it﴾: its meaning has already been explained in *al-Baqarah* (the Surah of the Cow).
